planting.note: Best fall-sown or cold-stratified for 60 days before spring sowing, as seed benefits from winter chilling to break dormancy; established plants tolerate dry summers once roots are set.

directions: A tall, aromatic mint-family perennial native to sagebrush steppe, dry meadows, and open forest edges across the interior western US, bearing whorled spikes of pale lavender to white tubular flowers that are heavily worked by native bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds through mid to late summer. The crushed foliage releases a strong minty-camphor scent, and the coarse, nettle-textured leaves give the plant its common name. It thrives in lean, fast-draining soils with minimal supplemental water once established, and resents heavy, poorly drained clay or excess humidity. Cut stems back in late winter to tidy dried seed spikes, which songbirds also visit through fall.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database

planting.note: Sow fresh seed outdoors in fall, since seed loses viability quickly and needs a cold, moist winter stratification period to germinate reliably the following spring.

directions: A high-elevation Appalachian endemic found on grassy balds, rocky outcrops, and open forest margins from Pennsylvania south to Georgia, distinguished from its wetland relative Angelica atropurpurea by smaller stature, purplish stems, and compound umbels of small greenish-white to pale purple flowers in late summer. It is an important nectar source for late-season pollinators and a larval host for black swallowtail butterflies. Give it cool, humus-rich, well-drained soil and dappled shade to part sun, mimicking the mountain woodland-edge conditions it favors in the wild; it struggles in hot, humid lowland gardens. Plants are short-lived and self-sow readily where happy, so allow some seed heads to mature and drop for succession.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in spring into consistently moist to seasonally wet soil; this floodplain species tolerates periodic inundation and actually depends on disturbed, open wet ground to compete successfully.

directions: A federally threatened floodplain perennial endemic to the Illinois and Mississippi River corridors, closely resembling a tall Michaelmas daisy with narrow leaves that appear to run down the stem (decurrent) and profuse white to pale pink-lavender daisy flowers with yellow centers in late summer through fall. It is adapted to riverine flood-and-drought cycles and does best in full sun on moist, periodically saturated alluvial soils where competing vegetation is kept in check by disturbance. In garden settings it performs well in rain gardens, pond margins, or any consistently damp low spot, and it draws abundant late-season bees and butterflies. Stake or pinch in early summer if grown in richer garden soil, since plants can become tall and floppy compared with their lean, flood-scoured native habitat.
sources: US Fish & Wildlife Service Species Profile

planting.note: Fall-plant container stock or scarify and hot-water-treat seed before fall sowing, since wild seed germinates naturally after fire-scarification and winter rains; avoid summer irrigation once established.

directions: A rounded, evergreen chaparral shrub native to dry slopes and foothills throughout California and southern Oregon, with small, rigid gray-green wedge-shaped leaves and abundant clusters of white to pale lavender-blue flowers that blanket the plant in early spring and draw large numbers of native bees and other pollinators. It is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established and demands lean, sharply drained, low-fertility soil; overwatering or rich garden soil quickly leads to root rot and short plant life. Site it in full sun on a slope or berm and give it plenty of room to develop its naturally dense, twiggy form, which also provides valuable cover and browse for wildlife. Avoid summer water entirely after the first year or two, matching its natural wet-winter, bone-dry-summer Mediterranean climate cycle.
